text: We expect this spending package to provide a fiscal impulse of 0.2-0.3%pt., which could go some way to alleviating the drag from the energy price shock and facilitate GDP recovery to a trend-like pace by 4Q26.
It's always sunny in tech economies

The trade data reports show that tech export momentum in Singapore and Malaysia accelerated in April, despite the Middle East conflict entering its second month (Figure 3). In Singapore, tech export strength has broadened from semiconductors to disk media and server-related products, underscoring the breadth of AI-related demand. Outside of tech, non-tech exports also picked up, propelled in part by equipment exports amid the ongoing global capex boom, including in tech facilities.
JPM Chase Bank, N.A., Singapore Branch

chart_caption: Figure 3: Tech exports - Malaysia and Singapore

text: Since the start of the Mideast conflict, we have also been paying close attention to regional energy trade, especially for Singapore given its status as a major refiner and Asia's largest oil trading hub (see note). In this regard, this week's trade reports show that not only did Singapore's oil trade volumes (both imports and exports) rebound from March lows, but Malaysia also experienced a surge in re-exports of petroleum-based products. Beyond price effects, this surge likely reflects trading partners' (and Malaysia's own) rush to secure energy-related supplies amid an unprecedentedly long blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. In sum, the April trade data not only gives us greater confidence that Singapore and Malaysia growth is likely to remain resilient in 2Q, but we also see upside risks to our 2Q growth forecasts if tech momentum continues at its current pace.

We continue to see the MAS and BNM remaining on a patient hold, but persistently solid GDP growth—if also accompanied by stronger inflation than we currently expect—would raise the odds of BNM policy normalization (i.e. 25bp rate hike) later this year. In particular, headline inflation in Malaysia remained low at 1.9% oya in April due to prevailing fuel subsidies which are absorbing a roughly 4%-pts hit to the CPI. But persistently high oil prices are putting increasing pressure on the government to rein in other spending and review its fuel subsidies.

1Q26 GDP surprised to the upside, led by gross fixed capital formation (GFCF; Figure 4), which also grew at the strongest pace in 13 years at 9.9% oya. Private consumption remained resilient, but energy headwinds are rising in 2Q26. The 1Q26 outturn supports our above-consensus GDP growth forecasts of 2.1% for 2026 and 2.5% for 2027, which are premised on our constructive post-election view on investment-led growth. We also see upside risks from the planned fiscal stimulus.
In terms of monetary policy, we still expect the BOT to stay on hold at 1.0% over the remainder of 2026. However, the brighter growth outlook could lower the growth hurdle for
4Q26 hikes. We continue to see a risk of hikes in 4Q26, by up to a total of 50bp, taking into account the medium-term inflation outlook.

list_items: - BoP pressures driven by capital account rather than current account
- PMI’s suggest margin compression in manufacturing
- Core IP softens in April, though unlikely to be driven by shortages

text: As we highlighted earlier, the weakness in the balance of payments (BoP) so far has been driven by subdued capital flows, despite the comfortable current account deficit (CAD). Looking ahead to FY27 (year ending March 2027), higher oil prices are expected to widen CAD sharply. These less supportive BoP dynamics are resulting in depreciation pressure on the INR.

This week's flash PMI continues to suggest that, amid limited pricing power, firms are struggling to pass through the sharp rise in input costs. While manufacturing activity appears to be moderating after strong growth in 1Q, the weakness looks cyclical rather than driven by supply shortages related to the Middle East crisis.

Manufacturing input prices rose for a third consecutive month in the May flash PMI report, reflecting an elevated cost environment linked to the Middle East crisis. However, output prices edged down in May. More broadly, manufacturing output prices have risen more modestly than input prices in recent months, pointing to weak pricing power among corporates (Figure 1).

chart_caption: Figure 1: Manufacturing PMI: Input and Output Prices

text: The April CPI report also showed core-core inflation remaining contained, rising by just 0.3% m/m (sa), underscoring the weak pass-through of cost pressures (Figure 2).

chart_caption: Figure 2: Core-core CPI

text: The flash manufacturing output PMI dipped marginally in May (to 56.6 from 56.9 in April). This follows a sharp drop in the output index in March at the onset of the Middle East crisis (60.7 in February to 55.7 in March). Other activity indicators, while softer, have not shown a decline of the same magnitude, suggesting the fall in PMI activity indices is largely sentiment-driven. Core industrial production (40% weight in IP) fell 1.1% m/m (sa) in April which translated into 1.7% oya (Figure 3).

chart_caption: Figure 3: Core IP

text: Given the size of the decline and the sectors involved, the weakness appears more cyclical than related to shortages. One exception was the fertilizer industry, which contracted sharply (-20% m/m, sa) in March due to gas shortages, before partially recovering (+10.4% m/m, sa) in April (Figure 4).

Separately, coal production fell sharply again (-4.4% m/m, sa in April) following a 4.7% contraction in March. This is occurring at a time when power demand has surged due to a heatwave. Recall that around 70% of India's power generation is coal-based.
